title: Counting by night
hookLine: during the Omer, the day's count is said at evening prayer

cards: Days till vacation. Sleeps till a birthday. Weeks till a baby is due.

A countdown makes waiting feel like it's going somewhere. For seven weeks every spring, from the second night of Passover until Shavuot, Jewish tradition keeps a different kind of count, out loud, one day at a time.
At the end of the evening service, the congregation stops, says a blessing, and announces the number. Today is twelve days, which is one week and five days. And then everyone goes home.

teach.h: SEVEN WEEKS SHALL THERE BE COMPLETE.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the day of rest, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the waving; seven weeks shall there be complete."

teach.h: THE OMER: A SHEAF OF BARLEY.
teach.b: The sheaf is the omer, a measure of new barley brought to the Temple on the second day of Passover. So the count is called sefirat ha'omer, counting the omer.
Forty-nine days, and on the fiftieth, Shavuot, the festival of the wheat harvest and, in Jewish tradition, of receiving the Torah at Sinai. Why count at night?
In the Jewish calendar, a day begins at sundown, and the verse says the weeks should be complete, temimot. Count in the morning and you'd miss part of the day.
Counting at nightfall catches each day from its very start, so it belongs to Maariv. One rule makes people careful.

Forget to count one night, and you can still count the next day, without the blessing. But miss a whole day, and many authorities say you keep counting for the rest of the weeks without saying the blessing.
The chain matters. And notice which way it counts. Not down, but up: not days left until Shavuot, but days already lived since Passover.
From freedom toward the Torah, step by step. Each number is a small claim: I was here for this one too.

how: From the second night of Passover until the night before Shavuot, the omer is counted each night after nightfall, usually at the end of Maariv: a blessing, then the day's number in days and weeks. Someone who misses a full day continues counting without the blessing, according to common practice.

counting the omer: forty-nine days to Shavuot
the barley offering brought on Shavuot morning

it counts up from Passover to Shavuot.
the count is said at night because a day begins at sundown
and the weeks must be complete.
missing a whole day usually ends the count
many keep counting, just without the blessing.

games.q: it's the spring, during the omer. you forgot to count last night, and the next day has now passed too. what does common practice say?
o: keep counting, but without the blessing.
count twice tonight to catch up.
games.why: many authorities say you continue the count without the blessing, because the chain was broken.

practice: Choose one thing you're in the middle of, days since you started something, weeks you've kept a habit, days on this path, and count it up, not down.
Say the number aloud the way the omer is said, today is this many days, and let each one count as a day you showed up.
